meta.description: Churchill used the joke, but did not invent it — it was an anonymous American newspaper gag by 1920, twenty-two years before the first Churchill attribution; the earliest known version is a May 1920 newspaper column.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'A good speech should be like a woman's skirt'?
meta.ogDescription: An anonymous 1920 American newspaper joke. A congressman used the speech version in October 1920; the first Churchill attribution is 1942.

answer.label: Not original to Churchill — an anonymous 1920 joke
answer.authorDates: Anonymous American newspaper joke · in circulation by 1920
answer.sourceLine: Churchill probably did use the gag — a New York columnist reported it in 1942 and a 1943 column reported Frances Langford hearing him deliver it in London — but he did not invent it. It was already an anonymous American newspaper joke by 1920, twenty-two years earlier: the earliest known instance is a May 1920 Buffalo newspaper column, printed in quotation marks, comparing a column to a woman’s skirt. Variants applied to a bathing suit and a manuscript follow within months. The earliest version applied to a spoken address is June 1920 (C. H. McNider, South Dakota Bankers Association convention); the earliest applied to a campaign speech is Rep. Richard N. Elliott in October 1920.

source.excerpt: A speech should be very much like a woman's skirt—long enough to cover the subject but short enough to be interesting.
trail: Earliest known instance: columnist Gerald K. Rudulph, in The Buffalo Enquirer of 21 May 1920, applies the skirt simile to a newspaper column — and prints it in quotation marks, which signals a saying already in circulation rather than one he coined the full chain ↗.

The earliest spoken version follows a month later: in June 1920 C. H. McNider, president of a Mason City, Iowa bank, tells the South Dakota Bankers Association convention his talk will be ‘short enough to be interesting, long enough to cover the subject’.
A contemporaneous variant compares a manuscript to a bathing suit: the Asbury Park Evening Press of 30 July 1920 runs ‘short enough to be interesting and long enough to cover the subject’.

Applied to a campaign speech, the line was used by Indiana congressman Richard N. Elliott on 26 October 1920. The earliest Churchill attribution appears in a New York column in 1942, twenty-two years later, in the ‘lady’s dress’ form; a 1943 column reported Frances Langford hearing him deliver it in London.
source.excerptNote: The earliest known form applied to a campaign speech (a bankers’-convention talk by C. H. McNider predates it, June 1920). Elliott did not present it as his own invention either — by late 1920 this was simply a joke going round, which is exactly the condition in which quotations lose their authors and later acquire famous ones.
source.rightsNote: Free to reuse. The originating texts are anonymous American newspaper material from 1920 (with related 1881–1908 antecedents), published well before 1930 and therefore in the public domain in the United States; you may reproduce the 1920 wording in full. Because the joke is not Churchill’s, his estate’s copyright to 2035 is irrelevant to it. The one thing to avoid is quoting the 1942 columnist’s reported Churchill phrasing as though it were a verified Churchill utterance — that is a journalist’s paraphrase, and it is his text, not Churchill’s. This is not legal advice.

author.name: Winston Churchill
author.heading: Why it gets pinned on Churchill
author.metaLine: 1874–1965 · British statesman, historian and Nobel laureate in Literature
author.bio: Sir Winston Churchill is the great attractor of orphaned witticisms: any remark about oratory, brevity or wit drifts toward him eventually. In this case the drift had real help, because he probably did use the joke — which makes it a subtler problem than a pure fabrication. Using a joke and originating one are different things, and quotation sites almost never distinguish them.

misattribution.heading: The attribution problem
misattribution.intro: A more interesting case than the usual fake, because the credit is not simply wrong. Churchill probably did use a version of it — reported by a New York columnist in 1942 and, in 1943, by a column describing Frances Langford hearing him deliver it — but two decades after everyone else.

items.who: Used by Churchill, not coined by him
items.why: The first Churchill attribution is 1942, in a New York column reporting him. The joke is documented from 1920, so he was repeating a stock gag that was already circulating long before his premiership the chain ↗.

items.who: A newspaper column, then a speech
items.why: The earliest known form (May 1920) compares a newspaper column to a skirt; a July 1920 variant compares a manuscript to a bathing suit; only by October 1920 does it settle on a speech.

Skirt or dress or bathing suit; ‘create interest’ or ‘be interesting’ or ‘be attractive’; applied to a speech, a sermon, a letter or a column. There is no canonical form because there was no original author.
Ronald Knox is sometimes named — usually for the sermon version. Quote Investigator found no substantive evidence he used it.

misattribution.truthLine: An anonymous American newspaper joke in circulation by 1920 — used by a congressman that October, and not attributed to Churchill until 1942 the evidence ↗.

context.heading: Why it resonates
lead: It survives because it is genuinely useful advice about speaking, smuggled inside a joke — cover the material, then stop. Advice that arrives as a laugh gets repeated far longer than advice that arrives as a rule.

It has also aged unevenly. The gag depends on a 1920s frisson about hemlines that has largely evaporated, leaving a line that lands today more as a period piece than as wit — which may be why it now travels chiefly as a Churchill anecdote rather than on its own merits.
detailsBody: May 1920: a newspaper column compared to a woman’s skirt (Buffalo Enquirer) — printed in quotation marks, i.e. already circulating. The earliest known instance.
June 1920: C. H. McNider tells a bankers’ convention his talk will be short enough to be interesting, long enough to cover the subject — the earliest spoken version.
July 1920: a manuscript compared to an up-to-date lady’s bathing suit (Asbury Park Evening Press) — a contemporaneous variant.
October 1920: Rep. Richard N. Elliott applies it to a campaign speech.
1942: a New York columnist reports Churchill using the ‘lady’s dress’ form — the first Churchill attribution (a 1943 column adds Frances Langford hearing him say it).
The gap between the joke and the famous name: twenty-two years.
context.pull: He probably did say it. He just said it twenty-two years after everyone else.
